<reason>Both sides were disciplined, well-grounded, and responsive, but CON built the more concrete and durable case. PRO's strongest frame—the symmetry of two sticky, unchosen defaults—was crisply crystallized in the closing, but CON answered it head-on in both A1/A2 responses and the closing: tracking is code on a page the user opened and can already refuse, whereas the mandate is a statute conscripting every OS with a filter users rarely reverse, so it is not "restored control" but an unpriced cut. CON's mechanism arguments were sharper and went largely unanswered: the third-party-only block leaves first-party walled gardens intact (a moat, not a floor—PRO's "uniform floor" answer at A2.5 was refuted at B2.8 and never repaired), the liability/compliance burden on small browsers and open-source systems was only thinly deflected, and the spam-filter analogy was effectively distinguished (spam filters do not decide which publishers may fund a page). PRO's answers to the pressure questions (A4.1–A4.2) were direct and labeled, but the rebuttal was clipped mid-sentence, a small execution cost, and its final weighing relied on the assertion that an in-page "please allow tracking" ask is fully audible—CON's rejoinder that a buried system-settings trip is not a real ask held up better. PRO did land real hits (consent theater, the point that CON's data-rules fallback concedes regulation), so this is a clear but competitive win for CON, not a blowout.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was over list-writing and the spam-filter analogy: PRO (A4.1) argued existing blocklist ecosystems and platform liability make "robust" blocking an established function, while CON (B4.5) countered that spam filters eating an email do not decide which publishers may fund a page, that misclassifying a fraud check or CDN is the veto itself, and that liability is a tax small browsers cannot pay—an answer PRO never squarely repaired.</best_rebuttal>
